nameStory: The 'large-leaved' part of this plant's name is pretty straightforward - it has bigger leaves than most of its avens cousins! The word 'avens' comes from the medieval Latin 'avencia,' though the exact meaning has been lost to time. Some botanists think it might relate to an old word meaning 'to come' or 'to arrive,' perhaps referring to how quickly these plants establish themselves in disturbed soil.
description: Large-leaved Avens is a medium-sized wildflower that belongs to the rose family, though you might not guess it at first glance. This perennial herb typically grows 1-3 feet tall with a somewhat scraggly, open appearance. It produces small yellow flowers in late spring and summer, but it's actually more noticeable and distinctive when it goes to seed. The plant has a rosette of large, compound leaves at its base and smaller leaves along its stems.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The real showstopper - spiky reddish-brown spheres about the size of a marble, covered in tiny hooked bristles that feel like nature's velcro when you brush against them. These seed balls will grab onto your socks, pants, or pet's fur with remarkable tenacity.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves with several leaflets, where the end leaflet is noticeably bigger than the side ones. The leaves feel somewhat rough and hairy to the touch, with irregular, toothed edges that give them a jagged appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright yellow flowers about half an inch across with five rounded petals. They're not particularly showy and often seem almost modest compared to the dramatic seed heads that follow.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a basal rosette of large leaves with several branching stems rising from the center. The overall appearance is somewhat loose and open, not dense or bushy like some wildflowers.

habitat: Look for Large-leaved Avens in moist, partially shaded areas like woodland edges, stream banks, and disturbed forest soils. It thrives in rich, somewhat mucky soil and often pops up in areas where the ground has been disturbed by logging, trail maintenance, or natural events. You'll often find it mixed in with other moisture-loving plants in cool, damp spots throughout New England's forests.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the ground in a distinctive rosette pattern, with the large compound leaves unfurling as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Small yellow flowers appear from late June through August, followed quickly by the developing seed heads that will become the plant's signature feature.
seasonality.fall: The spiky seed balls reach full maturity and turn reddish-brown, becoming nature's hitchhikers as they cling to anything that brushes past. Leaves may yellow before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, but you might still find those persistent seed heads clinging to other plants or scattered on the ground where they've finally let go.

funFact: Those innocent-looking seed balls are such effective hitchhikers that they can cling to fabric for months - some hikers have found Large-leaved Avens seeds still attached to gear they stored away the previous season, ready to sprout in a completely new location!
confusionNotes: Most people confuse this with other avens species when it's flowering, since they all have similar small yellow blooms. The key is waiting to see the fruit - Large-leaved Avens has those distinctive spiky, reddish seed balls, while White Avens has smaller, less dramatically hooked seeds, and Water Avens has feathery, plumed seeds that look completely different.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the rose family, Large-leaved Avens doesn't look much like a typical rose - no thorns, very different flowers, and a completely different growth habit. This is a great example of how plant families can include surprisingly diverse-looking members that share important internal structures.
compareHints: Among New England's avens, Large-leaved Avens is the champion of seed dispersal with its aggressively clingy fruit balls. White Avens has much smaller, less hooked seeds, while Water Avens goes a completely different route with feathery, wind-dispersed seeds. The leaf size difference is usually pretty obvious too - this species lives up to its 'large-leaved' name compared to its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's avens species, white avens is distinguished by its small white petals and grabby seed heads.
Water Avens stands out among its relatives by being the wetland specialist with drooping flowers.
Unlike its avens relatives that grow in woodlands and meadows, Eastern Mountain Avens is the only species in its genus adapted to extreme alpine conditions in New England.
Among New England's avens species, yellow avens is the most common and widespread.
Rough avens is the scruffiest member of the New England avens family, with the most noticeably hairy and rough-textured leaves.
Wood Avens differs from our native White Avens by having yellow flowers instead of white ones and preferring shadier spots.
Among New England's avens species, Spring Avens stands out for its early bloom time and preference for consistently moist, rich soils.

Among New England's avens species, cream-colored avens stands out for its distinctly pale yellow to cream flowers - white avens has pure white petals, yellow avens has bright yellow ones, and water avens has drooping, bell-shaped flowers.

Unlike other New England avens which typically have upward-facing yellow or white flowers, prairie smoke has distinctive nodding pinkish flowers and creates the dramatic feathery seed plumes that no other regional avens species produce.

Scarlet Avens stands out dramatically from all other New England avens species primarily due to its bright red flowers - our native avens species like White Avens, Water Avens, and Yellow Avens all have much more subdued flower colors.
